chapter: Jamming, bootleg records and the Topsy hit
title: Royalties, Love Records and the follow-up 'Topsy' recordings
summary: Inexperienced backers botched the money; Cole recorded the follow-up LPs.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Did you ever get any royalties from it?

Oh yeah, yeah I got cheated out of some royalties, I'm so sorry that I couldn't make a hit record for a studio, an established, like a Decca or Victor or Brunswick or Columbia, somebody that was used to handling money. See, these kids weren't used to handling money and money was coming in too fast and it got all messed up with the government, you know, like that and it was just one hassle after another.
That's why it was called Love Records. That explains that.
See and they just wasn't used to it, thought it was easy to make a hit record. See, you don't make hit records that quick, you know.
What was the backer's name, the guy that asked you to do it?
Okay, well that explains something, because then it has for 1959, Cozy Cole with the Alan Hartwell Orchestra.

For Random Records. That explains that. Okay. On the Discography for that in Jepsen which is a dicography for records made after 1942, they have a whole series of titles listed. They have 'Topsy I' and 'II', 'Turvy I and II', 'Bad Charleston', 'Late and Lazy', 'Crescendo', 'Topsy Turvy I' and 'II', 'Afro Caravan', 'Deed I Do' and 'Topsy Too'.
When did you make all those, after the thing became a hit? " After "Topsy" was a hit, yes. After "Topsy" was a hit, so I made "Bad" and "Topsy" and "Turvy" and all those.
You put an LP out then.
So that's how a hit record was made, without you being in on it.
Anything at all. Just goes to show you.
